definition: Easily affected, harmed, or influenced by something.
example: Younger kids are often susceptible to peer pressure when deciding what to wear.
nuance: Susceptible suggests a tendency to be affected or swayed; vulnerable stresses being exposed to harm or attack.
prompt: A nurse explains why some patients at a clinic receive flu shots before others.
options: Older patients are more susceptible to the flu, so they get the shot first.
Because Marta is susceptible to the flu, she has never once caught it.
The nurse grew susceptible of the man who kept skipping his appointments.
The nurse gave a susceptible explanation that every patient understood easily.
reasons: People who catch the illness more easily are the ones who benefit most from early protection.
Being easily affected by an illness would make catching it more likely, not impossible.
This confuses the word with suspicious; distrusting someone is not the same as being easily affected.
The word describes something open to influence or harm, not an explanation that is clear.

practice.prompt: A gardener is deciding which tomato variety to plant this year.
options: A thick, susceptible stem held up the heavy fruit through every summer storm.
She skipped the heirloom variety because it is susceptible to leaf blight.
That variety is so susceptible to blight that its leaves never show a spot.
The gardener was susceptible that someone had been picking her tomatoes at night.
reasons: The word points to weakness against outside forces, so it cannot describe a sturdy stem.
Avoiding a plant that catches a disease easily is a sensible reason to choose another.
A plant that readily catches a disease would show signs of it; spotless leaves suggest resistance.
Here the word is mistaken for suspicious, which means doubting or distrusting.
